# Zhuangzi: Garden of Sayings, Volume 3

<margin>This describes the conduct of the <term>Zhiren</term> <gloss>Perfect Man</gloss> who does not seek fame or prominence. Why then do you find joy in being known?</margin>
He rebuked him: "The Perfect Man is not known. Why do you take joy in fame?" Confucius said, "How excellent!" He gave up his social circles and dismissed his disciples.
<margin>He does not value ostentation.</margin>
He fled to the great marshes, wearing skins and coarse cloth and eating acorns and chestnuts.
<margin>He does not value delicacies.</margin>
<margin>Because he did not give rise to a mind of discrimination, he did not disturb the groups of birds and beasts.</margin>
He walked among the beasts without disturbing the herd and among the birds without disturbing their flight. If birds and beasts did not dislike him, how much less would humans?
<margin>Even different species did not dislike him.</margin>
<margin>The name of a hermit.</margin>
Confucius asked Zi Sanghu: "I was twice driven out of the State of <term>Lu</term>. The tree I rested under was cut down in the State of <term>Song</term>. My footprints were erased in the State of <term>Wei</term>. I was impoverished in <term>Shang</term> and <term>Zhou</term>. I was besieged between the states of <term>Chen</term> and <term>Cai</term>. Having encountered these many hardships, my close friends have grown more distant and my followers have scattered. Why is this?"

<note>A small symbol, possibly a printer's mark or seal, is located in the top right corner.</note>

<summary>This page records a dialogue between Confucius and the hermit Zi Sanghu. Confucius describes his many political failures and social isolation, seeking an explanation for his hardships from the perspective of Daoist detachment.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Zi Sanghu, Perfect Man, Zhiren, Lu, Song, Wei, Chen, Cai, hermit, social withdrawal, discrimination</keywords>
